lesson.title: From Farms to Factories: America Builds an Industrial Base
lesson.summary: Breaking from the colonial mercantile pattern of shipping raw materials abroad, American entrepreneurs built the country's first factories in the decades after independence, laying the industrial foundation that would transform the whole economy.
lesson.body:
Under British mercantilism, the colonies had been valued mainly as sources of raw materials, cotton, tobacco, timber, and furs, that were shipped to Britain and returned as finished manufactured goods, a relationship that deliberately discouraged colonial manufacturing so it would not compete with British industry. Independence removed that legal restraint, but it took decades, and some deliberate policy shocks, for American manufacturing to take off. The Embargo Act of 1807 and the War of 1812 cut off the supply of British manufactured goods, and Americans, unable to import what they needed, began building the factories that would eventually replace those imports for good.

Industrial textile production began almost by theft. British law forbade exporting the designs for its advanced spinning machinery, so when Samuel Slater, a young British textile mechanic, emigrated to the United States, he had memorized the designs rather than carrying plans. In 1793 he used that memorized knowledge to help build the first successful water powered cotton spinning mill in the United States, in Pawtucket, Rhode Island, launching the American factory system in textiles.

That early model expanded dramatically with the Boston Associates, a group of Massachusetts investors led by Francis Cabot Lowell, who built an integrated factory at Waltham in 1814 that combined spinning and weaving under one roof, and then a much larger complex of mills in the 1820s in a new town named Lowell after him. The Lowell mills famously employed young unmarried women, known as mill girls, recruited from New England farms and housed in company boardinghouses, a labor arrangement that briefly made industrial work seem respectable for women before working conditions worsened and immigrant labor increasingly replaced them.

Manufacturing innovation was not limited to textiles. Eli Whitney's cotton gin, patented in 1793, mechanically separated cotton fiber from its seeds and made upland cotton wildly profitable, which paradoxically expanded and entrenched slavery across the South even as it fed Northern textile mills with raw material. Whitney later pursued a contract to manufacture muskets for the federal government using interchangeable, machine made parts rather than hand fitted components, an approach that, though Whitney's own results were mixed, pointed toward what became known as the American System of Manufacturing.

This new industrial base depended on New England's deep tradition of literacy and skilled craftsmanship, the same educational inheritance that would soon nourish the Transcendentalist writers of the same region, since mechanics, mill managers, and machinists needed to read technical instructions and adapt designs rather than simply follow rote habit. By the 1820s and 1830s, factories, machine shops, and a growing class of wage laborers had become permanent features of the Northern economy, setting the stage for the sweeping economic transformation historians call the Market Revolution.
